title: Intervals
summary: Sort ranges by their endpoints and sweep through them once to merge, count, or schedule overlaps.
lesson:
How it works
- An interval is a start and an end. Two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends; whether touching endpoints overlap depends on whether the ranges are open or closed.
- Sorting by start (or by end) puts related intervals next to each other, so a single pass can resolve overlaps.
- Sorting costs `O(n log n)` and usually dominates; the sweep itself is linear.

When to reach for it
- The input is meetings, bookings, time ranges, or segments on a line.
- The question asks to merge ranges, find conflicts, insert a new range, or count how many overlap at once.
- You need the fewest removals or resources so that ranges stop overlapping.

Common patterns
- Sort by start, then compare each interval with the last one you kept.
- Sort by end to choose greedily: keeping the interval that finishes first leaves the most room for the rest.
- Sweep line: turn intervals into start and end events, sort the events, and keep a running count.
- Already sorted input: copy the ranges before, absorb the overlapping ones, then copy the ranges after.

Pitfalls
- Getting the boundary rule wrong for intervals that only touch.
- Sorting with `a[0] - b[0]`, which overflows for extreme values; use `Integer.compare`.
- Mutating the caller's array when the contract says not to.
- Forgetting to emit the final open interval after the loop.
